section_summary: This section combines 1946 occupation-era press translations with late-1947 and 1948 diplomatic reporting on Japanese politics, economic recovery, food rationing, labor, and public opinion. Early items discuss the purge ordinance, the Social Democratic Party, constitutional revision, and Marxist criticism of the emperor system; later despatches summarize Japanese reactions to communist victories in China, war-crimes judgments, political scandals, elections, economic stabilization, and rice-delivery quotas. The section also contains a Far East Command press release and correspondence concerning acquisition of a historical run of the Mainichi Shimbun.

subfiles.title: Press Translations No. 824, Political Series No. 199: Purge Ordinance, Social Democratic Party, and Emperor System
subfiles.from: Allied Translator and Interpreter Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Translations and summaries of Japanese press items concerning the purge ordinance, Social Democratic Party deliberations, and constitutional treatment of the emperor system.
subfiles.summary: Press Translations 824: a proposed ordinance implementing the purge directive, a Social Democratic Party meeting postponing the presidential question and qualifiedly backing the emperor system, and a call to face the emperor system during constitutional revision.

subfiles.title: Press Translations No. 862, Political Series No. 209: “The Emperor System” by Hachirō Noguchi
subfiles.from: Allied Translator and Interpreter Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Translation of a Mainichi Shimbun essay interpreting the emperor system as an alliance of absolutism, landownership, capitalism, militarism, and bureaucracy.
subfiles.summary: Press Translations 862: Hachirō Noguchi argues the emperor system protected landlords and the bourgeoisie, tracing absolutism from the Meiji Restoration, and concludes expansion in China failed to preserve its social base.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Distribution of Japanese Press Translations
subfiles.about: Request that the Japan-Korea economic office receive its own copy of GHQ's Japanese Press Translations series.
subfiles.summary: Martin encloses a sample of the Japanese press translations and asks how his office, responsible for Japan and Korea economic affairs, can get a dedicated copy.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Comment on the SCAP Press-Release Despatch
subfiles.about: An internal handwritten note assessing a despatch that summarizes an attached SCAP press release.
subfiles.summary: Partly illegible annotation says the despatch adequately summarizes the SCAP material it transmits.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 14: Press Release Concerning Corrective Rationing Measures Taken in Hokkaido
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmission of a GHQ announcement on improved distribution of supplemental food rations to Hokkaido coal miners.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 14: five copies of SCAP's J. C. Twinem statement on Hokkaido rationing; supplemental foods limited to miners finishing a full day or meeting quotas, with stronger incentives for underground workers.

subfiles.title: General Headquarters Far East Command Press Release of 23 December 1947
subfiles.from: Public Information Office, General Headquarters, Far East Command
subfiles.about: A multi-item military press release containing Christmas messages, Hokkaido rationing news, a typhoon report, personnel announcements, and operational notices.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur and senior Army and Air Force commanders issue Christmas messages praising occupation service and urging continued dedication to peace. A rationing item details measures linking Hokkaido coal miners' supplemental food to attendance, job classification, and production, while another reports Typhoon Jean west of Yap. Further items name enlisted men selected for officer candidate school, announce General Gairdner's return to Tokyo, and describe a destroyer's unsuccessful search for the drifting Kyuko Maru.

subfiles.title: Letter Regarding Purchase of a Mainichi Shimbun Collection
subfiles.about: Inquiry whether the Library of Congress wishes to buy a nearly complete Mainichi Shimbun run held in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Schuler reports a Mainichi Shimbun collection from June 17, 1917 to the present available for 400,000-500,000 yen, about $1,000, in good condition; he asks the Library of Congress for an early decision.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 709: Japanese Reaction to the Fall of Mukden
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Analysis of Japanese press and political reactions to the Chinese Communist capture of Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Sebald reports widespread Japanese anxiety that communist successes in Manchuria, Korea, and Indonesia could encircle Japan and encourage domestic communism, especially in Hokkaido and Kyushu. Conservative and mainstream newspapers treat Mukden's fall as a major threat to East Asian security and Japan's economic recovery, while Akahata celebrates the victory. Sanzō Nosaka attributes Communist success to mass support and superior leadership and predicts a new Chinese coalition regime based on Mao's program. The despatch concludes that regional events were transforming Japanese communism from an abstract concern into a perceived immediate danger.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 775: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending December 9, 1948
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Weekly summary of Japanese editorials on war-crimes appeals, Yoshida's policy speech, and the supplementary budget.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers warn against treating the United States Supreme Court's consideration of war-crimes appeals as grounds for leniency and emphasize collective Japanese responsibility for the war. Papers across the political spectrum condemn Prime Minister Yoshida's Diet address as vague, election-minded, and lacking constructive policy. Economic journals and major dailies similarly criticize Izumiyama's budget presentation, although the despatch notes that press attacks overlook occupation authorities' role in delaying Diet dissolution until essential legislation and appropriations were passed.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 788: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending December 16, 1948
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Weekly survey of press reaction to Finance Minister Izumiyama's misconduct, party politics, corruption, and war-crimes jurisprudence.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo press treats Izumiyama's drunken behavior and advances toward women Diet members as a symbol of the legislature's declining dignity, extending blame to politicians and the electorate. Newspapers also discuss Ken Inukai's election as Democratic Party president and prefectural demands to purge corruption following Ashida's arrest. Magazine commentary on the Tokyo war-crimes judgment stresses Japanese collective responsibility and the prevention of future aggression, while legal scholars question the tribunal's use of newly developed international-law doctrines.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 806: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending December 23, 1948
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Weekly review of editorials on the American economic-stabilization directive, labor restrictions, Communist criticism, and developments in China.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers broadly accept the necessity of the American economic-stabilization program while regretting that their government had failed to implement similar principles earlier. Editorials recognize that austerity may restrict strikes and other labor rights, and several urge unions to subordinate demands to national economic recovery. Akahata attacks the program indirectly through criticism of a single exchange rate, low wages, taxation, food collection, and restricted credit. Limited commentary on China suggests that Japanese opinion was beginning to consider accommodation with an expected Communist victory.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 818: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending December 30, 1948
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Weekly summary of Japanese editorial reaction to the execution of Class A war criminals, the coming election, economic controls, and rice quotas.
subfiles.summary: Editorials on the execution of seven major war criminals emphasize that their deaths do not absolve the Japanese people of responsibility and should instead strengthen Japan's commitment to peace. Newspapers then shift attention to the January 23 election, clean politics, minor parties, labor restraint, and the political implications of the American stabilization directive. The final portion examines anxiety over pre-planting and possible additional rice-delivery quotas, noting that low official rice prices and rising farm costs could provoke resistance among farmers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 10: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending January 6, 1949
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Opening page of a weekly press survey focused on foreign affairs and year-end assessments of Japan's occupation and recovery.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 10: press reaction for the week ending January 6, 1949 on China, Congress, Truman's address, reparations revision and elections, with year-end editorials crediting the Occupation while urging Japan to own democracy and recovery.
